utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone in the courtroom. Could the court officer please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-5/18-T, the Prosecutor versus Radovan Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam. Your Excellencies, and ladies and gentlemen. Today we are holding a motion hearing to discuss several binding order motions filed by the accused. There remain seven of these motions pending concerning Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, France, Germany, Iran, Italy, and the Netherlands. The accused and the states in question have filed various written submissions in relation to them. Following a Status Conference held on 28th January, the Chamber determined that it would be helpful to hear from the representatives of these states and the accused at the hearing to be held today. Representatives of the seven states were invited to attend today's hearing; however, following further submissions from the accused, it was determined that it was unnecessary for representatives of Italy to be present at this time. Similarly, on 10th February, the Netherlands informed the Chamber that of the two outstanding documents to be delivered to the accused, one would be provided before the hearing and that it was making urgent arrangements with regard to the second. As a result, the Chamber was of the view that representatives of the Netherlands should also be excused from the hearing. Finally, on 12th February, Friday last week, Bosnia and Herzegovina informed the Chamber that due to "technical obstacles" it was unable to organise its representatives and send them to The Hague in time for the hearing. The Chamber would like to express its disappointment that this is so and would like to emphasise that hearings such as this one conducted pursuant to Rule 54 bis are held for the benefit of the states rather than any other party. At such hearings, the states can be heard before a determination is made by the Chamber on whether they should be compelled to disclose documents to any of the parties before the Tribunal. Given that Bosnia has failed to use this opportunity, the Chamber would proceed to consider the accused's motion concerning Bosnia without hearing from its authorities. We are, therefore, sitting today in the presence of the accused, the Prosecution, and representatives of Croatia, France, Germany, and Iran. I would like to thank the state representatives on behalf of the Chamber for their attendance and their contributions to this hearing. Let me first introduce the members of the Trial Chamber to you. I'm Judge O-Gon Kwon from South Korea. To my right is Judge Howard Morrison from the United Kingdom; and to my left, Judge Melville Baird from Trinidad and Tobago; and to my far right, Judge Flavia Lattanzi from Italy as a reserve Judge. I would now like to ask each of the representatives to identify for the record who they are and which state they are representing at this hearing. I will follow the alphabetical order. For Croatia first.

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you turn on the microphone when you speak, and I was told, Ambassador, this is the first time ever in the history of the Tribunal that five languages are interpreted at the same time, so to make a pause between each statement. Please go ahead, Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. My name is Josip Paro, and I'm Ambassador of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ambassador Paro. For France.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. Jean-Luc Florent, deputy director of legal affairs in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. MS. DE MATHA: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Ginette de Matha, Chargee de Mission with the direction of legal affairs in the foreign affairs ministry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RENAULT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Celine Renault, Chargee de Mission in the defence ministry in France in the direction of legal affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. VILLEMAIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jacques Villemain, Legal Advisor with the French embassy in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And then for Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAUFER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my name is Thomas Laufer. I'm Ambassador of Germany here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRAUTMAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, my name is Sebastian Trautman. I represent the Ministry of Justice in Berlin.

utterances.speaker: MS. ACHILLES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. My name is Susanne Achilles. I'm the second secretary in the legal department of the German Embassy in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And lastly for Iran, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ESFAHANINEJAD
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, my name is Mahmoud Esfahaninejad, deputy for legal and international affairs of the embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOKHBEROLSAFA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, my name is Ali Mokhberolsafa, legal advisor to the embassy of Islamic Republic of Iran. MR. SABERI ANSARI: Thank you, Mr. President, my name is Behzad Saberi Ansari. I'm the legal counsel of the embassy of the Islamic Republic of Iran in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Karadzic, I see that you are again here on your own and I understand you will not be joined by any of your legal advisors today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat with your microphone on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we hearing interpretations?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would like to greet all the Excellencies present here. As for my presence here on my own, this is how it should remain until the end of this hearing. Concerning my associates, I have two of them at the moment, one of them in The Hague, and in fact I do not need them for this particular section of our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Can I also have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Alan Tieger, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff, and Iain Reid appear for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Before we move into the submissions, there are a few procedural matters that should be addressed. As you know from the Scheduling Order issued last Thursday, 11th of February, each of the accused's motions will be discussed separately, with only the representatives of the state concerned present in the courtroom, together with the accused and the Prosecution. That means that following my opening remarks, I will ask the representatives to leave the courtroom, with the exception of the representatives of Germany, who will be heard first. Following the discussion of the motion hearing and motion relating to Germany, those state's representatives will leave the courtroom and the representatives of France will come in and we will deal in turn with each motion in this manner. How the submissions are being made, the representatives of the states not in the courtroom are free to observe the hearing from the public gallery. They will be able to see and hear everything unless we go into private session to discuss confidential matters, in which case the audio will not -- will be turned off. I was also told that there are two witness rooms in the back of the courtroom where the representatives of the state which is to be heard next can wait until they are asked to come into the courtroom if they so wish. The next matter I want to deal with is any application for a private or closed session hearing. Given that much of the filing in relation to this hearing are public and that many of the states have made no mention of national security issues in their filings, the Chamber has decided that it will proceed in public session until a specific issue requiring us to go into a private session arises. It is for the representatives concerned to notify the Chamber when they believe we have reached the point and the Chamber will then consider whether a private session or closed session is necessary. If the Chamber decides to go into private session or closed session, those watching the hearing in the public gallery will not be able to hear what is being said in the courtroom, nor will the hearing BE broadcast to the public. In addition, those portions of the transcript that are in private session will not be available to the public. Indeed, only the parties and the state concerned will receive a copy of those portions of the transcript that are in private session. I note also that on 10th of February, 2010, Germany filed a notice of objection, reiterating its position that the binding order motion concerning it should not be granted on the basis that the accused has not satisfied the requirements of Rule 54 bis. I'm explaining this in the presence of representatives of all states concerned as a way of introduction of the structure of the Rule 54 bis procedure. However, should the Chamber decide otherwise and grant the motion, Germany requests that it be granted a reasonable period of time to assess which documents, if any, will raise national security concerns. Once these are identified, Germany will seek a number of protective measures pursuant to Rule 54 bis (F). Given that these are all measures which are to be considered in the event of the Chamber granting the motion, the Chamber does not consider it necessary to go into private session for the purposes of today's discussion. Much of that discussion will be concerned with the requirements of Rule 54 bis rather than a detailed analysis of certain documents. However, as I said above, if the representative of any states are of the view that a specific issue should be discussed in private session, they should inform the Chamber accordingly. If any representatives have any questions about this, please feel free to raise them now. Then there's another matter. As you know, the Chamber has invited the Prosecution to attend this hearing. Unless the accused or any representatives request the discussion of a particular issue or document to be heard ex parte, the Prosecution shall be here throughout the hearing and have access to the transcript of the hearing. In this regard, I would like to know if there are any objections to that from the representatives of the states or the accused. I see none. Finally, before we begin, I would like to note that this hearing is scheduled to last one morning session only, during which we intend to hear all the representatives of the attending states as well as the accused. Accordingly, I would strongly encourage everybody to focus on the main points of contention rather than outlining all of the arguments already made in the writing -- in the written filings. All submissions are to be addressed to the Chamber and we will give the appropriate party the opportunity to respond when necessary. Of course, given that Bosnia has chosen not to send its representative, we can be a bit -- a little more flexible with our schedule issued on 11th February and can allow extra time, if necessary, to the participants in the hearing. I would also like to note that we have decided to start with Germany, as the issues arising from that motion are quite different to the issues that need to be discussed in the remaining motions. Following Germany, we will hear from France and have a break, and after the break Croatia and Iran will be heard in turn. During each separate hearing, the accused will be asked to make his submissions relating mainly to whether there have been any developments since the last Status Conference. After that, the floor will be given to the representatives of the states to make their submissions. The accused will be given an opportunity to reply and the Chamber may also ask questions. We shall have a ten-minute break now in order to escort the state representatives, other than Germany, from the courtroom; but before that if there's any question in relation to procedural matter, I will hear them. I see none then. So the representatives of Germany are therefore free to speak in their own language because we have a German interpreter, as I said, and then we shall adjourn now for ten minutes for the arrangement. --- Break taken at 9.55 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. -- Ambassador Laufer. The Chamber notes that the issues arising from the binding order motion involving Germany are somewhat different to the issues we will discuss in relation to other states. This is because Germany is disputing that it should provide the accused with the documents requested in his motion, as falling under categories 1 to 7 on the basis that they are not relevant and/or necessary to the accused's trial, which is one of the requirements of Rule 54 bis. In this regard, the accused has submitted in his reply brief of 28th September, 2009, referring to the Appeals Chamber's ruling that a state does not have a standing to challenge relevance of the documents sought. However, the Trial Chamber is of the view that Appeals Chamber's ruling should be interpreted in such a way that it is ultimately for the Trial Chamber to decide whether or not the specific material sought is relevant and necessary, and that once the Trial Chamber has determined that the material sought is relevant and necessary, states are not allowed to challenge the relevance or necessity of the material. Therefore, the Chamber is of the view that it can be assisted by hearing from the states on the issue of relevance and necessity, until it finally makes its decision on the issue. It is for this reason that Chamber ordered the Prosecution to file its submission on the issue of relevance. So having said that, I wonder if you, Mr. Karadzic, have any observation to this issue. If you are of a different view, please elaborate on the point that the Chamber should not hear from Germany on the issue of relevance and necessity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not object to the Trial Chamber hearing the arguments of the state, which is reluctant to provide the necessary documents. However, the fact is that it is up to the Trial Chamber to be the judge of that. And my arguments will clearly show that all the documents in question are indeed necessary. For various reasons they're relevant, they're necessary, because they're going to show not only what happened on the ground and who we were dealing with, who the Serbian side was dealing with and what it had to face, which armed force it had to face, and what the scale of all that was. They will also show that the state members of the United Nations violated the arms embargo, that they -- that the witnesses from those states, the state members of the United Nations, were very dubious objectivity and impartiality, that impartiality in Bosnia and Herzegovina on the part of many states was also violated, that members and representatives of the United Nations and members of the United Nations were on the side of a warring party rather than neutral parties. I would like to hear His Excellency, the ambassador of Germany, and I'm very grateful to him and his associates for being here today. However, I am also prepared to provide arguments about the relevance and necessity of all the documents that the Defence has requested. I would also like to confirm that we wanted to avoid encumbering the Trial Chamber further, but the fact is that this is of the utmost importance for the entire war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and primarily for the conduct of the representatives of the international community, or rather, some of the states' representatives of the international community. And there is no way we can establish the truth without such documents. I am prepared to discuss each and every motion and explain why each of the documents is both relevant and necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we will hear from you, Ambassador Laufer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAUFER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, indeed on two occasions in our letters dated 25th of September, 2009, and also dated 10th of February, 2010, we asked that the submissions of the defendant are not admitted because we believe they do not fulfil the requirement arriving from Article 54 bis of proceedings, and hence it's still not clear to us because Mr. Karadzic is facing the accusation of genocide and other crimes, and it is not clear why it should be required. And we stick to our position. We ask that the defendant to limit him to happenings -- and that we shouldn't go back to political events between 1991 and 1995, because otherwise this trial is going to be political academy and it's not going to be a Tribunal. So this is my position as far as this case is concerned. Of course, all in all we checked and made sure whether there should be documents regarding to the demand made by the defendant, but we did not see that especially in his -- what it says in number 1 to number 7, that there should be such relevant documents, that they should exist. Of course there are conferences about -- and meetings about such relevant documents, but the documents that we have pertain to national security or pertain the protection of third states. And we cannot disclose that without the permission of those third countries. There's also the question of the German Parliament. The German Parliament is a democratic organ of the Federal Republic of Germany and it's autonomous, and you can also see Mr. Altmaier -- you got a letter from Mr. Altmaier where he makes an explanation about this. The Parliamentary Control Committee is going to convene in about six to eight weeks' time and they're going to deal with this question once again, and we might possibly also have a further notification from that particular body. Your Honour, if in case, if the Chamber accepts the motions under number -- Articles number 1 to 7, we already said in our letter on -- dated 10th of February, we need enough time in order to look into the matter as to which documents would be within the remit of the federal government and which would be relevant for a disclosure. And what we have seen so far, it does not apply in any of the cases, and we have also, in as far as the Rules of Procedure and Evidence clause 54 bis is concerned, we need to talk about this again. I just want to state quite clearly that in order to make the proceedings quite quick, that we believe - also in the interests of the Prosecution - that the disclosure should be limited to be -- to actual deeds because I don't think we're talking about the political state of affairs in Bosnia at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador Laufer. Mr. Karadzic, would you like to respond to this briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I absolutely do not agree with what His Excellency, the German Ambassador, has just stated. The events in Bosnia and Herzegovina were not part of a vacuum; they were provoked by certain circumstances. Those events were impacted by all the sides and all the parties, and there were at least four parties involved: Serbs, Croats, Muslims, and the international community. And within the international community, as the proceedings are going to show, we had individual states which were present there with their troops and their intelligence services that acted independently on behalf of their governments because we, ourselves, did not allow any state to act on its own behalf. We also had member states of NATO and some of their staff worked for the NATO, not for the United Nations. As far as the issue of genocide is concerned, genocide is mostly linked to Srebrenica, although this has also been extended. The issue of the smuggling of weapons that arrived through Germany from -- and departed from Ramstein airport in Germany, that is of some significance. That issue has a lot of significance and will impact on the testimonies of international witnesses and UN member states that violated the arms embargo imposed on Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm prepared to deal with every issue and with every document. I'm not going to mention the name of the gentleman from B and D [as interpreted], I don't want to go into private session, but it must be of some concern what that gentleman did in the military observers' mission and at the same time he was a member of the intelligence service of Germany. These things have to be dealt with. We don't have to talk only about who killed whom in the civil war. Those countries knew that, they knew of all that, even when they heard -- before they heard of Karadzic, that even predicted that there would be 250.000 victims. We have to see now how come that the number of victims was smaller. We can absolutely not arrive at a full picture and have a fair trial and a fair sentence if we do not have all the elements and if such important countries as Germany do not appear. I'm not saying that I'm going to say what certain American officials did, even unbeknownst to their government during Tito's era. Not only did those countries predicted what would happen in Yugoslavia and especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Some of them were actively involved in the break-up of the former state of Yugoslavia and contributed actively to what would happen there. But this is not the issue at hand here. At this moment these are the most specific things that need to be discussed, and even these things from 1 to 7 and even 8 are very specific requests and the proceedings would not be complete and would not be fair without them. If Your Excellency is interested in each particular item, I am prepared to explain to His Excellency, the German Ambassador, why each of them is important. Not only did we defend ourselves from the entire world or from the Western part of that world, to be more precise, because they had their troops within the Bosnian army, not only were many resolutions violated, particularly the arms embargo --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's deal with it one by one. Let's start with item 8 you just referred to. Germany submitted that it couldn't find any item in relation to item 8. Do you have any say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if we're talking about the same thing, you're referring to the transcripts of the statement and the intercepts of my conversations. Well, I assume that Germany should have them because they have done -- worked a lot on this. They should have something, some intercepts on my activities related to Srebrenica, in view of the fact that they also had intelligence personnel on the ground. So they should have some knowledge as to what was happening. I did manage to find one intercept which is actually of exculpatory nature, which was provided by Croatia. But I would like to know what else there is out there because I'm sure that I haven't received all of it. In other words, I have to assume that Germany must have such documents because there was a lot of German presence there, both in the UNPROFOR and on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any substantive material that would substantiate your allegation that Germany should have more -- any material in relation to that category?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this particular case, item 8, I don't have any such substantial evidence, but it would be very unlikely that Germany, as one of the main actors in the events in the Balkans, does not have any documents. But as for the other items, of course I do have such supporting documents -- evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One of your arguments on relevance is that these documents are relevant to your count, Count 11, of taking hostages. What can you say about the claim that whether the UN personnel was combatants or civilians is irrelevant to the charges under Count 11? What is your observation to this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency and Your Honours, the Defence will dispute the position that armed representatives of international forces, whose commander is -- whose commander is the commander who issues orders for bombing, that such personnel should be considered civilians. In -- also the participation of such personnel in fire correction, in fire control and so on, who were on the ground, we will show that they were there. They were present. But what I would like to say is that the taking of hostages, which is charged under charge 11, was not something that had been ordered; it was done spontaneously and in panic. What I'm trying to say is that people perceived these representatives, these armed representatives, of the international community as biased. It's not only their perception; they were biased. So it isn't just that the people perceived them as combatants of one of the sides in the hostilities. They actually were part of the hostilities and they did side with one side in the conflict, and that is what we are going to show. And of course there was such a perception, but if that perception among the people was actually grounded, if we can show here what all the things that were -- all the measures that were taken on behalf of one side and taking one side, that cannot be considered as being unbiased. That is in flagrant violation of international law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your last comment leads me to the issue of the -- next issue of the credibility of international witnesses. When you are saying that these documents are relevant in assessing -- to the assessment of credibility of international witnesses, do you have specific witnesses in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would not here name the witnesses, but two of them are ambassadors, for instance, the two US ambassadors, and the US supported the violation of the arms embargo that was imposed on Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were in contact with the Bosnian and Croatian governments as well as the Iranian government via Croatia. They took an active role in providing a huge amount of weapons and military equipment and provided support, significant support, to one of the sides in the conflict. So how can we consider their representatives to be unbiased when their states were biased? The Excellencies here will speak or testify to the guilt of the Serbian side based on words, not an deeds. But ambassadors of a country that was actually involved in the violation of the arms embargo and was an interested party in the outcome of that war, the length of that war, and its intensity, how can we expect them to be unbiased witnesses here, the representatives of such states?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I leave the matter there. Finally I would like to touch upon the issue of Srebrenica -- just a second. Oh, yes, Ambassador Laufer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAUFER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Chairman, if you allow me, I would like very briefly to comment on the conduct of the defendant here because what he's just said is typical for the way he assesses documents, numbers 8 and 11, items 8 and 11 of the motion, which we've just heard explained in somewhat greater detail. He's working on the basis of assumption. He's simply claims that certain people whose names obviously he's obviously reluctant to give us had precise knowledge of certain events. Nobody can possibly check up on this, but he uses such an assumption as the basis for instigating research in all sorts of archives which a country has which cost a lot of time and effort is something which I find very inappropriate under the circumstances. I'd also like to point out that item number 11 where it's talking about a parliamentary investigation, which also pertains to the behaviour of German intelligence officers, is an issue on which the German Bundestag, the parliament, has decided that there are no documents that have ever existed on this and that, if possible, there may only be a sort of result of an internal discussion ever put on paper, and that, of course, is to be seen as strictly confidential, highly confidential document concerning the rules governing confidentiality of documents in Germany. I would also like to mention that the way the defendant has explained himself is not exactly helping us to motivate us to accede to his demands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ambassador Laufer, to be just clear, when you refer to number 11 it refers to the paragraph number of the accused's motion, not the item number itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAUFER
utterances.text: It was number 8. Your Honour, just a second. [Interpretation] Mr. Chairman, it is 7, indeed, I was wrong, you are right. It is 11, not 7. I had another document and made the mistake. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador Laufer. Now I turn to the issue of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, could I say a word, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very briefly, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not confine my request to item 8. Much more significant are items 1 through 7. The Austrian government actually pointed to the Government of Germany and they told us that the German government actually conducted investigations at the TWRA, which was actually a company that was a mask for the arms sales to Bosnia and Herzegovina. We've never disclosed anything that wasn't relevant. I would appreciate it if we could look at all the previous seven items, they're very significant, and they deal with very important information; and without them, it could not be considered that the accused was actually given an opportunity to defend himself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it the German government is well aware of your request. Now back to Srebrenica. In this regard I would like to ask the Prosecution the following four questions. Although they submitted in their prior submission, so I wonder whether Prosecution is in the position to answer the following questions, whether the Prosecution challenges the following four facts: Number 1, Srebrenica was not demilitarised; 2, ABiH forces in the Srebrenica enclave launched attacks from the -- from inside the enclave; 3, arms were smuggled into the enclave; and finally 4, the ABiH -- ABiH forces in the Srebrenica enclave were legitimate military targets. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, to the best of my knowledge, the Prosecution has addressed these issues in its previous submissions, alluding to the pre-trial brief, perhaps to the opening statement, to the adjudicated facts that were submitted, and certainly acknowledge that, again, as indicated in our previous pleading, that those are -- the Prosecution was not asserting that the enclave was demilitarised, as we said here; the Prosecution does not dispute that arms were present in and smuggled into the Srebrenica enclave after it was declared a safe area; that the enclave was not demilitarised; and that attacks by Muslim forces from within the enclave against Bosnian Serb forces and villages continued after the establishment of the Srebrenica safe area. So I don't think that issue is a matter of dispute, as we pointed out more than once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to be clear, Mr. Tieger, as to the number 4. You mentioned in your brief number 1 to 3, but I don't remember having heard from you on number 4, whether -- I speak again, whether the ABiH forces in the Srebrenica enclave were legitimate military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I don't think we've ever taken the position that military forces are not legitimate military targets, so I think that was implicit in our previous submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I now turn to Mr. Karadzic. In light of the concessions by the Prosecution you just heard, can you explain to the Chamber why you find it necessary to obtain all these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I appreciate the acknowledgement by the Prosecution as to the truthfulness of these four items, which leads us to the conclusion then - and we can draw that conclusion today - that the decisions that I made or the Republika Srpska army in relation to Srebrenica were legitimate. However, that charge remains in the indictment. There is another issue here, there is the issue of the surrendered arms, we knew that there -- the origin of the arms. There is an arms factory in Tuzla, but we know that this -- these weapons were not from Tuzla, but rather from elsewhere. So we had to follow the channels in order to find out where all these weapons came from, which sides, and who all actually participated in all these events that caused so much trouble, including at the time when the Cutileiro Plan was being worked out. We have to see what actually happened then. But the fact remains that the charge in the indictment remains and I am charged with taking action against Srebrenica, although it is quite clear that we did not even intend to enter the Srebrenica enclave. We actually wanted to leave a way open for them to leave the enclave. What Mr. Tieger is saying, that there were attacks there in fact, I have to say that these attacks were really very, very violent. We had evidence that some of these fighters from the Srebrenica enclave returned to the enclave with a chain of Serb ears around their necks. We have to establish all the facts of the events and actually shed full light on the events in Srebrenica. So it is very important where the weapons came from and it is important because we want to show and we want to question how unbiased can representatives of such countries be as witnesses in this trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it is one thing that there's a legitimate cause in waging a war, but it's totally a separate matter how it is waged. So in this regard, Mr. Karadzic, I would like to remind you that the purpose of this trial is to judge whether you are guilty of charges as alleged in the indictment. And this is not an opportunity for you to produce a white book of all the events that took place at the time. And I would advise you to concentrate on defending yourself against the charges in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I will do my best --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say was that what the Prosecution conceded with regard to all these four questions relating to the enclaves, and this also applies to the conduct of the ABH or Muslim army. And this is very useful and helpful and is going to simplify the whole procedure and relieve some of the burden from the Defence in order to prove certain things. However, the fact remains that the sources of the weapons that arrived were in many countries that support this Tribunal who hold me responsible for many things and whose high representatives will appear here, either as Prosecution witnesses or I shall have, myself, to call some of them. In addition to the significance of the conduct of the BH army - and we are happy to see that this has been acknowledged - the conduct of all other participants in our war is equally important. That involves the procurement of weapons, transportation, and delivery and subsequently distribution of weapons throughout Bosnia-Herzegovina. All of this, of course, contributed to the duration of war. We would have ended the war much sooner had not only one side been persuaded and convinced that they could have everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's it. Thank you. I have a very short question for Germany. Although the practices and standards may vary depending upon the countries -- states and then the fact that one country adopts certain regime does not necessarily mean that the other countries also follow that. But just for consistency, in relation to category 6, Ambassador Laufer, the -- I will not name it, just in case, my understanding is that some countries are providing with those -- such documents to the accused or to the Chamber. So I wonder whether the thing is that Germany is concerned about its national security interest or that it has to do with the domestic law which does not allow co-operation with the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAUFER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we do not have a reason not to co-operate with any parties in the proceedings. I would like to emphasise that. For one thing, the motions made by the defendant are not sufficiently detailed. The defendant wants to have everything, wants to have all the documentation that has ever been written about the various subject matters. And -- but you can also look at the newspapers or the news agencies. He can ask for their reports. What we need -- what we are lacking is the selection mechanism in order to locate the documents that would be relevant, and documents that would be relevant. But what we've seen so far only just shows that either the government doesn't have such documents, there might be other institutions, or it might be the security services or other agencies. And secondly, we're not sure that those documents exist and they might be highly classified, top-secret level; hence, we cannot disclose them. And I've already submitted those two reasons, and in my opinion they still apply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador Laufer. The Chamber will confer briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I see the time. Ambassador Laufer, if you have anything further to raise, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAUFER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would suggest that my colleague would clarify one matter that has already been mentioned as well, if you allow him to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Of course. Mr. Trautman.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRAUTMAN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I would like to point out one thing. The accusation is about Srebrenica and events running it, and as you already asked the Prosecution as to how far there were military activities in Srebrenica. And the accused himself said in his motion under number 9 of his explanations, has pointed out that Bosnian archives have shown as to how far arms were delivered to Srebrenica. And in this respect, the motion is not clear because it's -- he always refers to arms being transported to Srebrenica with the help of German troops or NATO troops. But the question is how far arms have reached Srebrenica, if at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic, do you have anything to raise with respect to Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately, I have to express my disappointment. A study produced by the Dutch government has established that the Turkish and Malaysian members of UNPROFOR had smuggled weapons valued at $15 million --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not the time for you to repeat what you said already. I see the time. Now I would like to invite the French representatives --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may I say a word only, just one sentence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry I have to say this, but I would kindly ask His Excellency, the German ambassador, to bear in mind that both Secretary Warren Christopher, President Clinton, Lord Carrington, and all French high officials have identified Germany as some party which is very much responsible for the events that took place in our country, and I'm going to pursue this line of providing evidence that this is the case. And I don't know why documents that I requested cannot be provided to this Court without any prejudice or any jeopardy for Germany.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's it. Ambassador Laufer and Mr. Trautman and Ms. Achilles, thank you for coming to the Tribunal. Now you may be excused. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may make one point in response very quickly to a couple of the comments that were made before the representatives of Germany depart.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's only as a -- taking off on the point that the German representatives were making that there's -- pointing out the gap between the issue raised by the accused of arms coming into the country and whether or not they reached Srebrenica. There's also the further risk of conflating what was known at the time with what can potentially subsequently be accused -- be established. The accused has referred to various perceptions, the perception of people who were involved in taking hostages, the perception of arms being present in the Srebrenica enclave before a military operation was launched. These documents have nothing to do with that perception; it's what was known at the time that the accused has raised as a gap between these documents that are being sought and what was known. And we have -- we need to avoid a situation, which appears to be present here, where the accused seems to be saying: If I had only been aware of certain secret documents at the time, that I might have had a basis for launching a legitimate military operation or for a further perception about the status of the people who were taken hostages. So I urge the Court not to fall prey to that distinction. The issue is perception at the time, what was known at the time, and not what the accused may subsequently attempt to prove through documentation that he clearly didn't have at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. Before that I'd like to clarify with the audio/video unit that whether we can go further 50 minutes without any break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just briefly, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no secret, as far as we are concerned, that this weapons and this equipment did indeed arrive in Srebrenica. That's why these two enclaves were linked, which was contrary to the agreement on enclaves. Helicopters used to come to Srebrenica. The four documents provided by the Bosnian government only confirmed the arrival of the weapons in Srebrenica. As for the question that His Excellency has asked, whether it had actually arrived, it was being confirmed by the Bosnian government. We knew that as well because this weapons were used to shoot at us and to kill us, and we were aware of these helicopter flights. That's why we shot them down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That's it for Germany. Thank you again, Ambassador Laufer. Now I invite the French representatives. FRANCE

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning again, Mr. Florent, Mr. Villemain, Madam de Matha, and Madam Renault. Mr. Karadzic, in your memorandum of 8th of January this year, and at the last Status Conference, you indicated that you received one document from France but that you believe that France has more documents that should be provided to you. Also, I understand that you have agreed on the application of Rule 70 conditions to the one document you received. I'd like to hear from you now that whether there have been any developments since.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing happened in the interim period. As you know, on the 2nd of June and on the 30th of June and in the beginning of January I wrote about this issue relating to France. I believe that France was a very important player in our crisis. They had a significant presence, particularly in the area of Sarajevo, and their presence was manifested in a variety of ways. Even President Mitterrand visited the airport in Sarajevo, for which we are grateful because by that he demonstrated that the airport was safe for landing. This was followed by 10.000 sorties bringing humanitarian aid which considerably improved the humanitarian situation in Bosnia. Generals such as de Lapresle and Gobillard, who are well-known, were directly and fully informed about the situation. I think that every single request that I made and every single paragraph contained therein is something that I need to explain further, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will give the floor to the representatives of France.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. On an introductory note I would like to remark that France and its government has also co-operated and will continue to co-operate with the Tribunal. Our country contributed actively to its inception since we are a member of the UN Security Council. I would like this to be quite clear from the outset. As far as we are concerned, we are fully aware of this obligation to co-operate, which is ours pursuant to the Statute of the ICTY and the Rules of Procedure and Evidence of this Tribunal but also as regards the French law which applied to the disclosure of documents in this case. And according to us, these rules and regulations in France cannot be simply dismissed. Now, as far as the requests and numerous applications are concerned stemming from the accused addressed to France, we have already provided, I believe, a number of answers. I believe that these answers do not seem to satisfy the accused, but as far as we are concerned, we don't have much to add, Your Honour, in light of what we have already disclosed in one way or another to the accused through the Tribunal. As you know, among those applications made by the accused, we can focus on three types of documents, A, documents which in light of their diversity and scope and for some of the documents are vague require and still require on our part documentary research to make sure that these documents exist, if indeed these do. And category items 1, 4, 5, and 11, as well as item 10, as this has been formulated in the application made by the accused through the Trial Chamber. The French authorities looked into these requests and conducted researches to that end. After this research work, we found a document relating to a meeting held by the French Ministry of Defence, American and German ministries of defence in Key West on the 4th and 5th of March, 1995. This document has been forwarded to the accused through a verbal note on 7th of December, 2009. We had sought protection pursuant to Rule 70 of the Rules of this Tribunal. As far as this category of documents is concerned, we have nothing else to offer at this stage, and in general terms not either, we have nothing else to offer the accused. There were also a number of requests that according to us were addressed wrongly to France, since these were documents that had to do with international organisations, namely UNPROFOR and third parties, third states, and NGOs. We feel that since these documents are not French and do not belong to France - because by definition these are documents that belong to the United Nations or one or other state - it was not up to France to provide such documents which are not in its possession. These were the requests on -- where the items listed under points 2, 7, 8, 9 of the accused's application. Your Honour, there are also a whole series of requests which are closely linked to a description, locality, and relationships with the French intelligence services. On this point we've been extremely clear and I shall remain extremely clear today as far as this issue is concerned. We feel that it is not for us to forward to the accused or the Tribunal documents which relate to the way in which our intelligence services in France are organised, and we feel we do not need to disclose any documents established by these services. The disclosure of such information would reveal the nature and scope of France's ability in the field of intelligence services as well as in which place and in what manner these services operate. This would amount to not abiding by this principle of respecting national security interests, and this substantiates non-disclosure of these documents. Pursuant to Rule 54 of this Tribunal and in light of the French law, communication of sensitive or confidential information is something we are not able to provide and cannot provide. In sum, as I have said in my opening remark, the French authorities, as is customary, wish to co-operate with your Tribunal but feels that in the present case it has met its obligation pursuant to Article 29 of the Statute in light of the accused's application. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Florent. In order to be clear, can I ask you whether it is your position that there are no further documents to be found with respect to categories 1, 3, 4, 5, and 11, and partly 10? So that one document you disclosed to the accused was the only one that can be disclosed?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That is indeed what I have said. It's the only document that we were able to disclose to the Tribunal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question was if you're not further searching for documents anymore?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have no ongoing research.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, with respect to the category 5, referring to the meeting in Key West, so are you satisfied with the material provided to you by the French authority?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My associates are in the process of analysing the document and comparing it with the information that we received from other sources. We will be able to speak about that at a later stage; however, I would like to say that we are grateful to whatever we have received in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And I now turn to Mr. Florent again. With respect to items 6, 9, and partly 10, which France said it could not disclose those materials due to security reasons. So I wonder whether France could advance its argument more specifically, bearing in mind that the Tribunal's jurisprudence on whether states can refuse to produce documents based on national security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. As far as the reasons for which we are not able to disclose potential documents because I did not say that such documents existed. I addressed this issue as a matter of principle. I explained that the only disclosure, if any, if these documents exist, would provide information, sensitive and essential information, to which the French intelligence services operate. And that is why we feel on the one hand that this has to do very closely with national security interests, and if we apply the Rules of the Tribunal and French law, we feel we have no obligation to disclose the latter. We are also not convinced of the fact that information of this nature would be exculpatory for the accused. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Lastly, the -- as for the documents allegedly originated from third parties, for example, UNPROFOR documents, can I ask whether they are in the possession of French government?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Among the documents that have been requested by the accused as regards the category you've just mentioned, I would like to give you a few examples. Item 2, for instance, the 15th and 16th of February reports established by General de Lapresle to be addressed to Mr. Akashi, Special Representative of the UN, as regards arms delivery in Tuzla. It is clear that on reading this request that this report is a report which the French authority were not an addressee and therefore were unaware of since this report was established by a French gentleman, that is right, General de Lapresle, but this was a document issued by UNPROFOR. This was addressed to Mr. Akashi. Therefore, this report was exclusively an internal report and belonged to the UN. There is no reason why this application should be made and this request be made to France. As far as item 7 is concerned, we are asked for all reports, correspondence, and memos relating to UNPROFOR staff, UN military observers, staff of the UNHCR NGOs between April 1992 with a view to providing equipment to the Muslims in Bosnia. There again our answer is likewise. The same applies to paragraph number 8. So we feel as far as these various requests are concerned, as I said in my opening remark, Mr. Karadzic addressed it to the wrong person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me be clear again, you do not deny the existence of such documents, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether this is a translation issue. I just indicated that these documents were UN internal documents, which were not addressed to France. So I don't see how France could be made aware of documents which were solely documents that were internal to the UN. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Maybe I can be of help in relation to item 2 on -- of the request to France. Many of the requests that were directed to the states were actually also directed to the Prosecution, and the Prosecution did provide the two items mentioned under number 2, and therefore there is no necessity for any other state to search for them any longer. Therefore, the accused, whenever we disclose something to him, we indicate to which of his requests this does relate. And if he checks, he can see that a lot of documents he has already received from the Prosecution and would not -- there would not be any necessity for any other source to provide that same document. And it's very clear in relation to item 2, but it's also in relation to many other items that were asked from states that he has received quite a number of documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In addition to item 2, can you help us, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff, understand what other materials in respect of other items the accused has received from the Prosecution so far.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we filed our further response to Karadzic motion for postponement of trial, we appended appendix C, and in this appendix you can clearly see which requests were directed to the Prosecution. They're completely listed there. And in the appendix A you can also see what we have provided. In relation to France, I can say that we also provided materials in relation to point 5. We disclosed materials in relation to point 7. We disclosed materials in relation to point 9 -- yeah, these were the ones in relation to France. Whether the -- whether there exists other documents elsewhere, we of course would not be able to know, but if the accused would check what he has received in relation to certain items, he could easily see whether it's really necessary to get the same documents elsewhere again or whether he need any more documents to a certain topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put that into a writing, that -- indicating all the documents disclosed by the Prosecution to the accused that would fall under each item requested by the accused by the binding order motions, covering all the states.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can do that, but it will take a bit of time because it's a lot of materials. So -- but we can do that relatively quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In the meantime I would like to ask Mr. Karadzic as regards item number 6, as an example, you are requesting documents that would indicate presence of French personnel in various international organs. Could you explain to us how relevant these documents are to your charges in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Excellence. I would like to say first and foremost, I have before me the pre-trial brief in which it is stated that joint criminal procedure in respect of Srebrenica depending on whether there were weapons there and whether there had been an attack. The Prosecution doesn't say whether such a joint criminal enterprise would have happened if Srebrenica had been demilitarised. France is a friendly state of the Serbian people and of the Serbian state, and it's uncomfortable for me to talk about that here. Your Honours, we agreed to the presence of the United Nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina; however, most Western countries, most NATO countries abused that opportunity and were present in Bosnia and Herzegovina on behalf of their own governments and on behalf of NATO. I understand and I appreciate that the issue of the functioning of the French secret services are a matter of national security and I'm going to respect that and I'm going to respect Rule 54 bis and Rule 70. However, let me say that not only did some countries have their intelligence services there illegitimately, without consent, they also had teams for anti-sniper activity, for the elimination of sharp-shooters, and so on and so forth. These are all very important matters. For example, when it comes to item 6 - and I can tell you the same for each item - the issue of Markale is very important because the French investigators arrived on site first. The other incidents around Sarajevo are also important, the sniping activities are also important. The French government is in possession of the evidence that the Muslims killed their own people by sniping, by other tools in order to accuse the Serbian army. What could be more relevant? How else could we establish the truth and pass a sentence if we do not have that evidence as well? How can we talk about four different joint criminal enterprises that I'm charged with? I can prove that none of them existed, but how can I do that when such obvious things that we know that the French government has we cannot be provided with. I cannot rely on newspaper articles, as the German ambassador stated. Newspaper articles, it is indicated that somebody said something or indicated something or confirmed something, but we need documents. The Trial Chamber is certainly not going to accord the same weight to the newspaper article as they will to an authentic document. You should believe me that several governments had parallel and autonomous presence of important intelligence and active military forces in our country without our consent under the guise of either humanitarian organisations or the United Nations. In this courtroom we're going to see that nothing was what it seemed, everything was different. Journalists, humanitarian organisations, the United Nations, all of those involved the presence of things and people that they should not have involved. We can take items one by one, but the fact remains and the Excellence has just confirmed that France and the French intelligence service was present there on their own behalf and that they have plenty of information. And we are kindly asking them to provide us with all that information, and I assure them that all the confidentiality measures will be applied to such information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have one clarifying question for the French representatives. When you said that you were not able to disclose documents related to the categories number 1, 3, 4, 5, and 11, to me it was a bit unclear what it meant. Are you saying that there are more documents but you are not able to disclose them, or that there are no more documents falling in those categories?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. What I have said is that we have conducted research at the time when we were seized of this request filed by the accused and transmitted by the Tribunal. After this research work, we communicated a document which is mentioned in paragraph 5. Therefore, we have no other documents to disclose. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Bench will confer briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'll give you the floor, Mr. Karadzic, after having -- after hearing from -- after giving the floor to the French representatives. If there's anything to raise at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. No, I have no other issue to raise or comment to make. We have listened carefully to what the accused has said and we had rather not comment such developments. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Florent. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you hear me, Your Honours? I would just like to point briefly something. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I just want to remind the accused that there may be protective measures and he has to be careful when he names certain witnesses here in the courtroom. He was very careful with other witnesses earlier this morning, and now he's using names. And that's -- he should reconsider. We will also file something for redactions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Uertz-Retzlaff. Please do bear in mind what Madam Uertz-Retzlaff indicated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I will do my best. I will refrain from mentioning names, but it is a fact that there will be a number of high officials, French officials, mainly from the military whose forces were part of the UN forces in Sarajevo and were the first to actually come to the incident sites where incidents were investigated. And Prime Minister Balladur actually disclosed - this was a public fact - he disclosed that there were documents showing that the Muslims actually attacked their own people. There is no reason to -- not to disclose that here because it's in public evidence, and we would like to express our gratitude to the French who actually had the stamina and the ethics to actually present facts in contravention of what was publicly or widely accepted. And, Your Honour, if necessary I can go through all the items of my list that relate to the French government and the documents requested from the French government and I can explain how they're relevant and significant. And I even have evidence where the Dutch government and other very responsible authors actually claim that these documents that we are seeking actually are in existence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Florent, do you wish to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. FLORENT
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no, I don't wish to respond to this question directly. I would just like to thank the member of the OTP for having recalled a number of rules which seemed to have been forgotten by the accused. I will not address these, but for matters to be quite clear I would like to say that the French general that has just been mentioned by the accused were not there representing France but were there as part of UNPROFOR and that is in that sense that they reacted and reported to UNPROFOR. This is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Florent. Unless there's other matters to raise, that would conclude the hearing with respect to French government. I thank you for coming to the Tribunal and thank you for your contributions. Now we will have a break of 20 minutes and resume at ten to 11.00, with Ambassador of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: REPUBLIC OF CROATIA

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's still before noon, so good morning to you, Ambassador Paro, thanks for coming again. Mr. Karadzic, at the last Status Conference you indicated to the Chamber that you have been provided with 15 documents requested from Croatia. You also expressed the view that they are only a small part of the requested documents Croatia can provide, and you indicate that you have not received any response to your letter of 7th January, where you requested a number of additional documents. Have there been any developments since that Status Conference in terms of your correspondence with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to express my gratitude to Croatia for their goodwill and for the provision of some of the documents, but since the last Status Conference to date we haven't had any new developments. And the only thing that I would like to add is that Croatia is one of the most significant states or countries which either under pressure from the United States or out of a desire to assist the Muslims was always or was in the fulcrum of all the supplies of weapons and materiel in different ways and, if necessary, I can explain what all those different ways were and I can -- and that is why we feel that Croatia is in possession of the documents that we requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. Ambassador Paro, I'll now give the floor to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I must say that we are not aware of the request of the 7th of January, so such a request has not been passed through the embassy, as it was the case with the other requests, to which we have responded with 15 documents. Also I have received the instruction from my government to say that while we stand ready to provide more documents if we have those documents, providing also that the request is more specific. We don't find the requests specific enough to conduct an effective search for those documents, but what we have passed on is what we have in our possession; anything else, we -- other documents we haven't been able to trace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find this strange that the accused's submission dated 7th January hasn't been served to Croatia yet. That can be checked out in the meantime. Before that, can I ask the accused whether you are satisfied with the items that you received in relation to categories 7, 9, and 10 of the requested documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to say that the Defence is really grateful to Croatia more for their goodwill shown rather than the outcome. We believe that the documents are more numerous and, to be specific, let me say this: Croatia did not make any remarks at the outset that we weren't precise enough. For instance, on the 2nd of June and then again on the 30th of June, I addressed a letter to Croatia. And then on the 27th of July, Croatia replied that it did not have those documents in their possession. But then later on it turned out that they did. So this is just by way of illustration. And we do need to have these documents provided. I have to -- I would like to add that on several occasions Croatia took a very responsible position. For instance, when the Bosnian army ordered long-range missiles, Croatia which suspected that this might involve chemical weapons and weapons that are actually subject to inspection, in that instance Croatia asked the United States to send an inspection team before such weapons were to be delivered to the Bosnian side. And the Ambassador approved that. So it is not possible that Croatia does not have those documents. Long-range missiles did -- were supplied to Bosnia and Herzegovina via Croatia, and later on they were to be used against Croatia. And Croatia in that instance addressed the United States, seeking inspections, and the inspection was actually conducted. So there is -- that is as much as I have to say regarding that. There are also numerous meetings with Ambassador Galbraith; with Minister Granic, the then-minister of foreign affairs; with President Tudjman; Nikica Valentic, the prime minister who actually visited Iran on a negotiations mission where they were to determine the best way to supply weapons to Bosnia and Herzegovina. So it is impossible that such documents are non-existent and I hope that Croatia will find a way and perhaps see their own interests in providing them. And I have to say that even at first glance it would appear that Croatia assisted the Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina significantly; but on the other hand, at second glance you can also deduce from that that, in fact, this only prolonged the war. Although their original intent was to provide assistance, and all of this before the Tuzla airport was opened, all the weapons, ammunitions, and equipment was actually funneled into Bosnia through Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, in its submission dated 27th of October, Croatia said that your requests were not specific enough, and Ambassador Paro reiterated that position again. So my question to you is whether you provided -- whether you provided any material that would -- in order to be more specific in your request.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]. [Interpretation] Your Honours, there are very precise dates here. There seems to be some confusion with channels, but it's all right now. There is completely precise information about the meetings. For instance, the travel and visit by Nikica Valentic, the Croatian Prime Minister at the time, who visited Iran, and there is indicated a date and the week. I believe it was around 30th of April, 1994. Then there are meetings with Ambassadors Redmond and Galbraith, meetings with Mr. Holbrooke. Names are indicated of two American generals who did go to an inspection mission to Croatia. You can't be more specific. The only thing we don't know is what they had for lunch; everything else is perfectly obvious. Now, as for categories, the Croatian government should indicate which categories of documents they have, and then we are going to be more specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here are the dates, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- this new item, seven items, are they the ones that would replace your previous request?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so, Your Honour. I believe it's all cumulative and that all the documents need to be obtained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So my question is -- I do not doubt that these additional requests relating to seven items are not specific enough. What I referred to as not specific enough by -- cited by the Croatian authority are related to the previous request. So what other additional material did you provide to the Croatian authority in order to help them find the -- locate the documents with more specific identification?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe you're right, in view of the fact that there are dates, places, and persons involved for every item. For instance, Tuzla, February and March 1995; then the Akashi meeting with a certain general from France, where they informed that fixed-wing aircraft were in Tuzla on the 15th of February; then there is correspondence between France, the United Nations, and other countries, followed by the arrival of Turkish representatives and the visit of Muslim and Croatian representatives to Turkey to negotiate the supply of arms to Muslims; the thing about Key West we received through a different channel. Then -- I'm sorry, I'm a bit lost in my papers. But then we have the 31st of March, in fact 10 February to 31st March, some 49 days, a rather narrow time-frame, in which a lot of things happened. Croatia is certainly aware of the C-130 aircraft shipment to the airport of Tuzla. Croatia is also aware of other forms of arms smuggling. It is indubitably aware of the meeting and correspondence on the 29 April 1994 between Ambassador Galbraith, Ambassador Redmond, and President Tudjman, which marked an intensification of American activity. It is well-known that at the beginning of the war in 1992, the United States protested, and on the basis of their protest one arms shipment was seized at the airport. Later the United States changed their position in order to encourage and support Croatia, if not even force Croatia to be more responsive to requests. Nikica Valentic visited Tehran in April 1994. Ali Akbar Velayati, the foreign minister of Iran, was in Zagreb in May 1994. Merhamet should be a humanitarian organisation but it was a cover, in fact, for arms smuggling, and it worked through Croatia. It had a very important base in Croatia. So there are five points on which Croatia is very well informed and sometimes involved. The delivery of arms to Tuzla, Iranian shipments of arms going through Croatia, other forms of arms shipments through the United Nations and humanitarian organisations, and then Croatia knows a lot about the bombing at Markale and it wire-tapped all our conversations. Croatia had a very good intelligence service and kept all our conversations under surveillance. Croatia needs to tell us exactly which items are insufficiently clear and need to be more specified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before I turn to Croatian representative, let me give you an example. Let's take a look at item number 7 in your -- of your first request, which reads: "All reports, memoranda, cables, and correspondence concerning the delivery, shipment, or use of arms obtained by Bosnian Muslims in violation of the United Nations arms embargo from April 1992 to August 1995 into the United Nations safe areas of Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde." Do you not find that a bit broad?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only at first glance, Your Honour. Namely, before the opening of the Tuzla airport, Croatia was a filter and a transit station for all these arms shipments, and Croatia took part of these weapons for itself. They know about each rifle, each bullet, each uniform, and each pair of boots that arrived, and they have records on that because it went through them. After the Tuzla airport was opened, perhaps they don't know everything, but before that they took one-third or one-quarter for their own needs and they must be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I turn to Ambassador Paro in terms of the issue of specificity. So if Croatia could suggest what sort of additional specification it needs to conduct its search. For example, could Croatian authorities not take the same approach they took when they singled out the previous 16 documents from the said web site in searching for the documents in their own database? Ambassador Paro.

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Your Honour, well, I have just been served with the copy of the defendant's letter of the 7th of January, following the receipt of the Chamber's invitation for this hearing. So we have seen the reference on this letter and we haven't been able to trace in otherwise quite ordered archives of our embassy receipt of such a letter. So I believe that this letter has never been served to my government. So -- and hence we couldn't have responded to the request in any way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll look forward to hearing from you on that submission, but we also have the previous request from the accused which is still pending. So we'll deal with it as far as we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Yes. So you must be aware of the response, and that is that the document -- the request is not specific enough -- well, it is always saying "all transcripts, all notes," it's very difficult to -- in some cases - I'm not talking about this letter of the 7th of January - to be very precise in trying to focus the documents. So all transcripts, all notes, say, for example, here we have all -- all transcripts, notes, or memoranda of the meetings between Minister Granic and Ambassador Galbraith of the United States at which the possible acquisition of arms from Iran was discussed. Well, where to look at -- I mean, that's not an easy thing, but I can't tell you what exactly -- what form of request, what explanation should be provided to us in order to find the documents. It's difficult unless we receive such a document -- such a request specified. So no idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: On a related issue, in Croatian submission you stated that the interested party will be able to search for such material, as suggested by the Croatian Homeland War Memorial and Documentation Centre. Could you elaborate on its meaning?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Not really, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Since it is the submission from the Croatian Homeland War Memorial and Documentation Centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
