utterances.text: I think it is rather clear what they are saying. So the memorial and documentation centre doesn't have those documents so -- or the documents of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who does the interested party mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Well, that is probably -- that refers -- at the Ministry of Justice who requested the documents, that interested party -- oh, no, well -- I'm sorry, I'm sorry. The interested party is referred to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I was wondering whether the Croatian authority would offer the Defence to look for the -- search for the document themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Well, it is said that the documentation centre is ready to give the list of documents, the list of documents and pass it on on the -- in their possession and pass it on on the Defence, which I think is rather generous offer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I will leave that there. Another question for you, Ambassador Paro, is whether Croatia is in a position to inform us whether the rest of the requested documents are in its possession or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: We have already stated that the rest of the documents are not in our possession, not as much as we are aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have any observation to the arguments advanced by the accused on Croatia's possession of requested materials?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: No. No, I have no comment on that. Because -- well, those are only presumptions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Another issue is the Rule 70 conditions. Is Croatia requesting these conditions pursuant to Rule 70 to apply to the document provided on November -- 9th of November?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Well, could you be more specific on the Rule 7?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Rule 70.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So what kind of conditions do you have in mind pursuant to Rule 70?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Well, I -- I don't know, actually, the Rule 70. What does it mean, the Rule 70?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: When you disclose the additional item on 9th of November --

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- the Croatian authority said "it was declassified with limited use." So I meant to ask you what the limited use would mean. Are you requesting for some protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Yeah, obviously. Obviously we would not want to -- these documents to be made public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And whether you are in a position to indicate to us how much time you would need in order to respond to the letter you just received, dated 7th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: Last time when we received a request for the documents, we have been -- we kindly asked the Chamber to give us a reasonable amount of time. So we are aware of the Court's tight schedule, but I have no specific period of time that we would need for that. Well, but certainly a reasonable amount of time, a month or so. Because -- well, those requests are rather general and -- and as indicated in our response, the archives are not always very tidy, especially those that do not concern the developments in Croatia proper. So probably it would require a bit of time to respond to those.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. The Chamber will confer briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless there are other matters to raise at this moment. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm convinced that we must do something about this. I understand what Croatia is saying, but if I may be of assistance, it would be important for us for someone responsible and high-ranking enough from the Croatian government under oath and on pains of punishment for perjury state that the meetings either did not happen or that they do not have the documents about those meetings. The Defence cannot accept that the states who should be co-operating do not co-operate simply by saying, "We don't have this." We don't agree they don't have this. For instance, concerning the 7 January communication, in one item we say Ambassador Galbraith and Ambassador -- and Minister Granic, Iran arms shipments. We don't need all the documentation. We just need the few documents concerning Iranian arms shipments between these people. Number 2, Ambassador Galbraith and President Tudjman, the moment when the green light was given for such shipments, that's April 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, Ambassador Paro stated that they didn't receive this letter, so I take his word and then there's no point of going into detail at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, but from the first point we can see specifically enough. We see that it's April 1992 to August 1995, but it's a fact that everything went through Croatia and Herceg-Bosna until the opening of the Tuzla airport and that Muslims gave the Croats in Bosna a cut. So they have to have information about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ambassador, would you like to respond to this?

utterances.speaker: MR. PARO
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Then it would conclude the hearing with respect to Croatia. I would expect the Croatian authority to do its best to co-operate with us in disclosing the documents requested in accused's letter of 7th January. Thank you again, Ambassador Paro, for coming to the Tribunal. Now you are free to go. So let us invite the representatives of Iran. Good afternoon, Mr. Mokhberolsafa. ISLAMIC REPUBLIC OF IRAN

utterances.speaker: MR. MOKHBEROLSAFA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just making sure you are following in the language you understand?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOKHBEROLSAFA
utterances.text: Yes, I will talk in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. So far, Iran has not delivered any documents to Mr. Karadzic, and instead has both argued that the requirements of Rule 54 bis have not been met but that it was not in a position to comment on this and ask for further extension of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOKHBEROLSAFA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As a result, the Chamber is not clear on whether Iran is continuing to search for the documents or not. So, Mr. Karadzic, in your memorandum dated 8th January, you stated -- you stated that you're still awaiting a response from Iran, and during the last Status Conference you were convinced that Iran was in possession of the requested documents. Have there been any developments with respect to Iran since?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. I have understanding for Iran, who find themselves in difficulties and under threat of sanctions, but I thought it would be one more reason for the Iranian government to supply all the documents that they have in their possession. They had requested several times -- in fact, there was no response to that item. In three months we have received no reply whatsoever. I have met all the requirements in terms of voluntary provision, and I would not like to resort to a request for a binding order. But it is a fact that Iran and the United States were quite in agreement about violating that resolution of the United Nations. And it would be useful perhaps to remind the whole world and the United States about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Now I would give the floor to Mr. Mokhberolsafa, if there's anything to add to what has been stated in your submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOKHBEROLSAFA
utterances.text: Yes, I briefly mentioned the statement of the Iranian government in reply to the motion as filed by the accused in this hearing. Actually, I -- to save time, I'm not going through the background to the motion. So I start with the issue of -- the issue that whether the requirement of Rule 54 bis have been met. Rule 54 bis stipulates that: "A party requesting an order under this Rule shall identify as far as possible the documents or information to which each application relates. Furthermore, this party must prove that the documents or information are relevant to any matter in issue in the proceedings before the Judge or Trial Chamber and necessary for the fair determination of that matter. In fact, the requirements set forth in this Rule are qualification of the principles introduced by the Appeals Chamber of the Tribunal in its judgement on the request of the Republic of Croatia for review of the decision of Trial Chamber of 18 July 1997 in Tihomir Blaskic case. As the government of the Islamic Republic of Iran has put forth in its previous notes to the Tribunal, which I draw your -- the attention of the Tribunal to note number 320-4/1711, dated 20 October 2009, the accused has not fulfilled his onus in this respect. The requested documents and information are ambiguous, very broad in nature, and therefore difficult to be identified. Also, the documents, if existing, are irrelevant to the case number IT-95-5/18-PT, that the accused is standing trial for. Despite all that, I will now describe briefly the voluntary efforts taken by the Government of Iran to locate and find the documents. In order to extend its highest degree of voluntary co-operation to the Tribunal, the Islamic Republic of Iran transmitted the request of the accused to its relevant organs. I would like to officially announce that the result of the search for the existence and validity of the requested documents was negative, and there were no materials in the documents that could be relevant to the charges against the accused. On the first class of the requested documents that covered a long period, starting from 1st April 1992 through 31st December 1995, no documents were found in our archives relevant to the claim raised by the accused. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that the Islamic Republic of Iran did not have any diplomatic relations with some of the mentioned states. On the second class of the requested documents, the relevant Iranian organs have responded that there is no trace with respect to the cargo manifests of the ships and aircraft after such a long time. All related documents including the bills of lading and cargo manifests are usually eliminated within limited period of time after the accomplishment of the delivery. Finally, with regard to the last class of the documents, almost all of the documents of the diplomatic relations between the Islamic Republic of Iran and Bosnia and Herzegovina have been screened and reviewed. I would like to announce that no documents containing materials relevant to the case initiated against the accused were found. Now I submit that the requested documents are not necessary for a fair determination of the case. One of the axiomatic principles of international law is the distinction between the jus ad bellum and jus in bello. The first corpus of law is related to a law of the use of force, while the second is regulated -- regulating the conduct of hostilities, in particular the means and methods which are permissible during armed conflicts. Even if one assumes that some states were supplying arms to the parties in an armed conflict, this fact in no way can justify the serious violation of international humanitarian law. Therefore, the requested documents are not necessary for a fair determination of the case as a matter of law. To conclude, for the reasons set out above the Islamic Republic of Iran is requesting this august Tribunal to reject the request of the accused pursuant to Rule 54 bis. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mokhberolsafa. In order to be clear, so you are today submitting not only that the requirements of Rule 54 bis have not been met in terms of relevance or necessity, but also that search has been completed on your part and that no documents have been found?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOKHBEROLSAFA
utterances.text: Based on the instructions I received and statement I just made to the Tribunal, it is my understanding that the search is completed and there is no further searches going on at present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. In his motion, the accused cites several publications or articles in order to support his argument that Iran must be in possession of the requested documents because it has been involved in supplying arms to Bosnian Muslims. So it's -- that I refer to footnote 2 to 8 of his motions. Can Iran comment on these publications or articles?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOKHBEROLSAFA
utterances.text: I regret to inform that for the time being we are not able to comment. We are not instructed to any further comments on the motion, and it's only limited to the statement which I just made to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Final question for you, Mr. Mokhberolsafa, is that Iran has also stated that it is not in a condition to comment on the merits of the request made by the accused. Could you explain more clearly what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOKHBEROLSAFA
utterances.text: As I'm instructed, that statement was at the time that the search was not yet completed, but now the search is completed. It is our understanding that no relevant document has been found.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I turn to Mr. Karadzic. Take a look at item 2 and 3 of your request, and item 1 as well. Most of them are relating to the events of time-frame in 1992, 1993, and 1994. How does the supply of arms during that time-period relate to or are relevant to the events in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not accused or charged with the crimes in Srebrenica alone, but also for my political activities starting in 1991 and onwards. In other words, it is not just about Srebrenica, although the weapons did arrive in Srebrenica although it had already been declared a protected zone. We -- what I would like to stress here is that we are not accusing Iran and Iran has no need to defend themselves. Let me put it this way: If the Prosecutor does not significantly alter the indictment and delete major parts of the indictment, they will actually put me in a position to defend myself -- to request more documents in order to be able to provide a defence. This process cannot -- or these proceedings cannot proceed as they should if we do not obtain documents from certain countries, countries that we are not accusing of anything. Your Honour, loads and loads of weapons, transports by ship and aircraft, were funneled into Bosnia from Iran, but they could not have been possible without the assistance of major players such as the United States or Croatia, which was the base for its distribution. And I think I have to reiterate several things here. First, these countries are claiming that some documents that I'm seeking actually belong or the source of those documents is a third party. But then I would appreciate it if they could provide us -- if they could point us as to where to search for those documents. And second, if this is the way it is going to be with the countries that were actors and significant participants in our crisis, then I would appreciate this Trial Chamber to subpoena high officials or to actually request high officials of these countries to state under oath that they do not have the documents that we are requesting. Because co-operation with the Tribunal is something that is a must, and my conduct, the duration of the war, the fury of the war itself and the resulting crimes that weren't really ordered by the commanders but rather by the chaos that was in place at the time -- so how can these sides, these parties, be excused from providing documents when they were participants in them -- of sorts themselves? So we have to have and find responsibility. Under items 1, 2, and 3, item 1 is perhaps a bit more general, but 2 and 3 are rather precise. There were people who were in place as of 4th September 1994 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, unfortunately you fail to answer my question. Take a look at item number 2, which includes, for example, "contents of the Iranian aircraft which landed at Zagreb airport, Croatia, on 4th of September, 1992; 1st of November, 1992; 4th of May, 1994 ..." How is this relevant to your case, even if it was done with the assistance of the United States or any country?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was done by people of -- who were people, flesh and blood, and who can be invited here to testify as witnesses. The weapons came from Zagreb, so this was a violation of a UN resolution, flagrant violation of a UN resolution. Secondly, the weapons arrived in Bosnia via UNPROFOR, which in that respect was a warring party, in fact, because it took sides with one of the warring parties. Through humanitarian organisations - and I don't mean just Merhamet, which was a Muslim humanitarian organisation, but many others who were there -- all of this actually provides a basis to -- for the Defence which can demonstrate that the charges put forth by the Prosecution are not as they seem. Because if you look at my pre-trial brief, I question there whether if all of these things had not happened, would all of the crimes that are later -- that the Serbs are later charged with occurred at all. If there had been no attacks from the protected zone, would there have been a response? So -- and if this was a legitimate response. And if there is no evidence that this would have happened had it not been actually provoked by vicious crimes coming from the protected zone, then we should show -- we have to be able to show that there is no evidence for this charge in the indictment. And the Serbian side was put in a position to defend their very survival and to act in a situation in which it was put, and not in fact to plan in advance all these crimes as the indictment and the Prosecutor claims. And if the charges remain, we have to have all these documents in order to be able to provide our defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will confer. One moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there anything further to raise, Mr. Mokhberolsafa?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOKHBEROLSAFA
utterances.text: No, I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, just to get it on the record, no, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, except that I hope that the Trial Chamber will actually protect my right to defend myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, then that concludes today's hearing. Thank you all very much for your attendance. The Trial Chamber expresses its gratitude for all submissions that have been made. We will consider them and give a decision in due course. Thank you. The hearing is now adjourned.
